title: Poverty and zakat today
hookLine: a blanket, a bowl and an axe: giving that lifts

cards: A man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asking for help. Is there nothing in your house? the Prophet asks. There is: a blanket, and a bowl for drinking water.
The Prophet sells them to people nearby and gives the man the money: buy food for your family with part, and with the rest, an axe head, and bring it to me.
He fixes a handle to it himself and sends the man out to gather wood to sell. The story is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud.

teach.h: A PILLAR: A SHARE OF WEALTH.
teach.b: Zakat, the obligatory alms, is counted among the pillars of Islam: a share of wealth, given by those who have enough, to those the Qur'an names. The list is in surah nine.

teach.h: THE ALMS ARE ONLY FOR THE POOR.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation it begins: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy," and goes on to name those who collect the alms, those whose hearts are to be won, captives to be freed, people in debt, the cause of Allah, and the traveler.
Notice how many are about getting someone out of something: out of chains, out of debt, out of being stranded.

teach.h: PURIFY THEM AND MAKE THEM GROW.
teach.b: A few verses on, the Qur'an tells the Prophet: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Purify and grow.

teach.h: FROM THEIR RICH, TO THEIR POOR.
teach.b: In al-Bukhari, when the Prophet sends Mu'adh to Yemen, he tells him to teach the people that zakat is taken from their rich and returned to their poor, in the same place. And today?

It is still calculated on savings, gold and business stock, and given through mosques, through charities and by hand. Some zakat funds pay off debts, or pay for a sick person's care, or help a family start a small trade.
Scholars discuss which uses fit the categories in the verse, and some debate whether zakat can fund long-term projects or should go straight to people. Behind the debate is the axe in the hook.
The hope is more than a meal.

teach.h: SO THAT NO ONE NEEDS TO ASK.
teach.b: It's the moment someone no longer needs to ask.

how: Muslims who have enough wealth calculate their zakat each year and give it through mosques, zakat funds, charities or directly to people in need who fall within the Qur'an's categories.

games.q: what does “poverty and zakat today” mean?
o: a voluntary tip given to beggars whenever you happen to see one
a government income tax collected in Muslim-majority countries
the share of wealth owed to those in need, meant to lift, not just feed

p: the Prophet fixed a handle to it
from their rich, to their poor
purify them and make them grow

s: the Qur'an leaves the recipients of zakat open
9:60 names them: the poor, the needy, the collectors, hearts to be won, captives, debtors, the cause of Allah and the traveler.
in Abu Dawud's story, the Prophet simply gave the man money
he sold the man's blanket and bowl, and had him buy food and an axe head to earn with.
the Prophet told Mu'adh zakat is taken from the rich and returned to the poor
so he tells Mu'adh in al-Bukhari: taken from their rich, returned to their poor.

games.q: a man comes asking for help. he owns a blanket and a drinking bowl. you're the Prophet. what do you do?
o: give him a meal and send him home.
sell his things, and send him off with food money and an axe.
tell him to come back next week.
games.why: the Prophet sold the blanket and bowl, told him to buy food and an axe head, fixed the handle himself, and sent him out to gather and sell wood.

practice: Bring to mind one gift you've given, or meant to, and picture what happened after it left your hands: did it feed someone for a day, clear a debt, buy a tool?
Don't grade yourself; just ask the axe question: could a gift help someone stand up, as well as eat? If you pray, ask for a giving that purifies and grows.

wordCard.voice: Poverty and zakat today. The share of wealth the Qur'an assigns to the poor, the indebted and the stranded, and the hope that it lifts people, not just feeds them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the obligatory alms given each year from wealth.

carryVoice: Your line: zakat can lift. A meal, and then a handle on the axe. See you tomorrow.
